title: Split Household Costs by Capacity
meta_description: Replace automatic 50/50 bill splitting with a transparent household system based on income capacity, unpaid work, ownership, autonomy and regular review.

sections.heading: Equal Dollars Are Not Automatically Equal Burden
paragraphs: A fifty-fifty split looks neutral because the arithmetic is simple. If two partners each transfer the same number, nobody appears subsidized. But equal dollars can create unequal burden when take-home income, debt constraints, childcare, health costs, employment risk or unpaid household work differ. One partner may fund shared life and still save; the other may fund the same amount by losing every margin for emergencies and retirement.

The opening photograph shows a couple with household papers and a calculator because the right question begins with the complete household system. What costs are genuinely shared? What income is dependable? Who owns each debt and asset? Who performs work that would otherwise require money or time? Fairness is not a universal percentage. It is an arrangement both people can explain, execute and revisit without hidden dependence.

A capacity-based split usually begins with income proportions, then adjusts for facts the formula does not capture. That does not mean the higher earner controls spending or the lower earner owes unlimited unpaid labor. Money contribution, decision power and personal dignity are separate questions. A sound agreement preserves voice, individual access to cash and transparent records for both partners.

This guide applies to married and unmarried U.S. couples, but legal consequences differ by state, title, account and marital status. A household spreadsheet does not determine property ownership, creditor liability or tax treatment. Use qualified local legal and tax advice for cohabitation, home ownership, marriage, separation or estate questions.
The goal is not to prove fifty-fifty wrong. Equal sharing can work when resources, obligations and preferences align. The goal is to replace an automatic rule with a documented test.

Before choosing a rule, each partner should complete the same private worksheet: income, required individual obligations, emergency cash, retirement access, credit constraints and the shared standard they can sustain. Compare worksheets in a scheduled conversation, not during a bill dispute. Differences are data, not admissions of failure. If disclosure reveals hidden debt or missing taxes, pause the split calculation and stabilize the underlying risk. A precise ratio built on incomplete facts creates false fairness and can expose both partners to housing or cash-flow shocks.

Set the conversation rules before discussing numbers. Each partner can request time to verify a claim, no one commits the household during the meeting, and disagreement does not authorize unilateral withdrawal of rent or essential support. Use a neutral worksheet and distinguish a temporary accommodation from the permanent formula. If the couple cannot discuss income, debt or ownership without intimidation, a more sophisticated spreadsheet will not solve the problem. Seek appropriate counseling, legal guidance or confidential safety support before increasing financial interdependence. The quality of consent matters as much as the ratio produced.

sections.heading: Define Shared, Individual and Negotiated Costs
paragraphs: Start with classification before percentages. Shared essentials usually include mutually chosen housing, utilities, groceries, household supplies and agreed childcare. Shared goals may include emergency reserves, travel or a home down payment. Individual costs can include personal debt incurred before the relationship, gifts, hobbies or separately chosen services. Negotiated costs are items with mixed benefit, such as a larger apartment needed for one partner’s child or a premium vehicle primarily used by one person.

Do not classify by who happened to swipe a card. Trace the economic purpose. One partner buying all groceries from a personal card is still carrying a shared cost unless the couple agreed otherwise. Reimbursements should follow the ledger, not memory. Likewise, a “shared” purchase should not be imposed after one person orders it.

Build a category table with owner, payer, beneficiary, monthly estimate, due date and split rule. Add irregular expenses—insurance, repairs, school costs, holidays and family support—so the arrangement does not appear fair only in an ordinary month. Convert known annual costs into monthly contributions or specify how they will be funded when due.

Set a threshold requiring joint approval. Below it, either partner may use the shared budget; above it, both agree before commitment. The threshold should govern contracts and recurring charges as well as one-time purchases. A low first payment can conceal a long obligation.

Revisit classification when circumstances change. A personal car can become the family vehicle; a shared subscription can become unused; caregiving can expand. Categories are decisions, not permanent truths.

Include family transfers and children from prior relationships explicitly. Support may be legally required, morally important or discretionary, but it still affects capacity. Decide whether visits, travel, school activities and gifts are personal, shared or partly shared. Avoid using the “individual” label to erase a commitment that shaped the household’s location or schedule. The classification should match the couple’s actual values while keeping legal responsibility accurate. Record disagreements as unresolved rather than quietly assigning them to whoever pays first.

sections.heading: Choose an Income Number That Measures Capacity
paragraphs: Gross salary is visible but may misstate spendable capacity. Begin with predictable take-home pay after required payroll taxes and mandatory deductions. Then decide how to treat voluntary retirement contributions, bonuses, commissions, equity compensation, business income and support obligations. The couple needs one definition that neither partner can manipulate by changing payroll elections.

A practical base uses ordinary net income before elective savings, then treats agreed retirement contributions as shared planning priorities rather than a private deduction from capacity. Another household may use net income after equal target retirement rates. Either can work if applied symmetrically and reviewed. Do not let one partner reduce the contribution ratio through optional benefits while the other funds current bills.

For variable income, use a conservative base drawn from a representative period. Fund fixed shared costs from the base and assign above-base receipts after they arrive. A quarterly true-up can correct reasonable differences without making rent depend on this month’s commission. Self-employed income should be net of legitimate business expense and include a separate tax reserve.

Disclose income ranges and timing, not necessarily every discretionary purchase. The [[S1|CFPB couples checklist]] recommends that both partners understand household income, expenses, debts, investments, accounts and bill systems so either can manage if responsibility shifts.
Review the income definition after a raise, job loss, leave, benefit change or new self-employment. A proportion built on stale pay is not neutral simply because the spreadsheet still calculates.

Benefits can create hidden capacity differences. One job may provide health insurance, retirement matching, paid leave or dependent-care benefits while another pays more cash. Do not assign a speculative dollar value to every benefit, but identify premiums and services that directly replace shared expense. If family coverage is deducted from one paycheck, add the shared portion back when comparing income or reimburse it through the bills account. Otherwise the providing partner appears to earn less because they already paid a household cost before take-home pay.

sections.heading: Calculate the Proportional Baseline
paragraphs: Add each partner’s defined monthly income. Divide each income by the total to obtain a starting percentage. If one contributes $6,000 and the other $4,000, the baseline is sixty percent and forty percent. Apply those shares to the agreed shared budget—not to every personal dollar. A $5,000 shared budget would produce $3,000 and $2,000 contributions in this illustration.

Use actual arithmetic but treat it as a baseline. If the lower earner has unavoidable medical cost, required support or a long commute created by the household location, an adjustment may be reasonable. If the higher earner insists on more expensive housing, the amount above the mutually affordable standard can follow a separate rule. Write the adjustment so it does not become a recurring argument.

Test remaining capacity. After shared contribution and required individual obligations, each partner should retain some personal cash and a viable route to emergency and retirement savings. A ratio that leaves one partner at zero is operationally fragile even when mathematically proportional. The household may need to reduce shared spending rather than keep refining percentages.

Avoid paying “percentage of each bill” manually. Set one monthly transfer to a shared bills account or ledger, then true up for variable categories. Automation reduces missed payments but both partners should see statements and maintain independent access appropriate to the account structure.
Recalculate on a stated schedule, usually after major changes and at least annually. Do not adjust for every small overtime shift; stability has value.

Document rounding and minimum funding. If the bills account needs a $1,000 buffer, fund the buffer using the same ratio or another agreed rule before reducing monthly transfers. Decide whether contribution percentages apply to shared savings as well as consumption. A couple may split required bills proportionally but fund equal personal retirement percentages separately. Run three cases—ordinary month, high-expense month and one-income interruption—to verify that the formula does not depend on perfect timing. A fair baseline should remain understandable under stress.

sections.heading: Protect Personal Cash and Equal Decision Power
paragraphs: A capacity-based system should not turn the higher earner into an owner and the lower earner into an applicant. Shared decisions need equal voice unless the couple consciously agrees otherwise for a narrow domain. Contribution percentage does not purchase voting percentage. Both partners should understand balances, obligations, goals and risks.

Preserve individual accounts or clearly defined personal allowances. Personal money lets each partner make ordinary choices without surveillance and provides resilience if a shared card fails. The allowances can be equal even when bill contributions are proportional, or they can follow another agreed rule. What matters is that neither person must request permission for every private expense.

Look for financial-control warning signs: hidden accounts or debts, withheld passwords to shared assets, forced signatures, monitoring every purchase, blocking employment, or threatening housing over disagreement. Those are not budgeting differences. A partner who feels unsafe should seek confidential support and avoid confronting control in a way that increases danger.

Maintain individual credit identity where appropriate. Joint credit accounts affect both borrowers, while an authorized user may not carry the same contractual liability. Confirm terms with the issuer. The CFPB notes that [[S5|joint credit accounts affect both partners’ credit scores]].
Fairness includes an exit path. Each partner should know which funds are individually owned, which are joint, which bills remain personally liable and where key records are stored.

Transparency does not require total visibility into every individual transaction. Agree on what must be disclosed: income used in the formula, shared-account activity, debt that affects household risk, tax obligations and commitments above the approval threshold. Preserve privacy below that boundary. Both partners should receive shared statements and alerts, and either should be able to describe the bill system. Cross-training protects the household if the usual manager is ill without converting mutual access into constant monitoring.

sections.heading: Count Care, Cooking and Household Operations
paragraphs: The midpoint photograph shows a father and child cooking because household capacity is not limited to paychecks. Childcare, elder care, meal planning, cleaning, scheduling, shopping, school coordination and emotional administration consume time and can replace paid services. Ignoring this labor while dividing cash by salary can charge one partner twice: less market income and more unpaid work.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics [[S2|American Time Use Survey]] measures paid work, household activity and childcare. Its current data show that care and household work occupy substantial time, especially in homes with young children. Population averages do not set a couple’s split, but they establish that unpaid work is economically relevant rather than invisible leisure.

Create a task inventory for one representative week. Record task, frequency, time, mental load, required availability and backup. Do not convert every hug or meal into an invoice. The purpose is to expose recurring operations and constraints. A person who remains available for sick-day pickup may carry a career cost not captured by active task minutes.

Choose a response: rebalance labor, outsource work from shared funds, reduce shared costs, or adjust cash contributions. Avoid an arbitrary hourly wage that pretends caregiving has one market price. Replacement cost, opportunity cost and fairness are different lenses; use them to inform negotiation rather than manufacture false precision.
Revisit after a birth, job change, school schedule, illness or caregiving need. The labor picture can change faster than salary.

Track schedule control as well as hours. A partner who can work uninterrupted while the other remains on call for school, deliveries or relatives receives a career advantage even if interruptions are brief. Rotate the on-call role where feasible and plan backup care from shared funds. Also measure rest: assigning every non-work hour to chores is not equitable because one salary is higher. The objective is sustainable combined labor and leisure, not extracting an identical number of minutes from two different jobs and bodies.

When paid help is considered, include payroll, scheduling and management—not only the advertised hourly rate. Outsourcing can still be worthwhile when it protects two careers or reduces conflict. Review whether the saved time is actually redistributed or simply absorbed by more work.

sections.heading: Build an Account Architecture, Not a Loyalty Test
paragraphs: Couples commonly use fully joint accounts, fully separate accounts or a hybrid. None proves commitment. A hybrid often uses individual income accounts, a joint bills account and joint savings for agreed goals. The structure should match transparency, convenience, legal ownership, creditor risk and each partner’s need for autonomy.

Before opening a joint deposit account, understand withdrawal rights and ownership. The [[S3|FDIC explains joint-account insurance rules]] for eligible deposits at insured banks, including equal withdrawal rights and aggregation within an ownership category. Deposit insurance treatment does not decide how a couple should divide money during separation or death; state law and account documents matter.

Set funding dates, minimum balances, overdraft settings and bill ownership. Decide whether both partners receive alerts and who corrects a shortfall. Keep shared emergency savings distinct from the bill account so an automatic draft cannot consume the reserve unnoticed.

Do not share passwords for individual accounts when the institution provides joint ownership, authorized access or view-only tools. Credential sharing can violate terms and creates poor records. Use each person’s own login and multifactor authentication.
Document what happens during incapacity, death or separation. An efficient account while life is calm can become inaccessible or disputed during transition.

Assign each recurring bill to an account and responsible reviewer, then create an exception process. If a joint balance is short, which transfer happens, who is notified and how is the cause corrected? Prohibit overdraft rescue from an individual account without notice. Keep copies of statements and ownership documents. If one partner dies or loses capacity, access can depend on title and legal authority—not knowledge of a password. Review beneficiaries and payable-on-death designations separately with qualified advice because they can alter the intended handoff.

sections.heading: Handle Variable Income Without Monthly Whiplash
paragraphs: When one or both incomes vary, a percentage of this month’s pay can create unstable bill funding. Estimate a conservative base from after-tax receipts over a representative period. Use that base for recurring contributions and hold excess in an income-smoothing account. Release a fixed owner draw or quarterly true-up rather than promising money before it arrives.

Define windfalls. Bonus, overtime, commission, tax refund and gift can follow different rules. A common sequence is taxes, depleted reserves, agreed goals, then personal allocation. The sequence should be written before the money creates competing stories.

Seasonal workers should map low months and renewals together. The shared budget must remain payable during expected troughs without using credit. If one partner’s stable income temporarily covers more, record whether that is a contribution change, reimbursable advance or shared response—not a silent debt that appears during conflict.

Review the formula using trailing evidence but avoid penalizing growth. If business income rises, increase the base after the pattern is established. If it falls, cut shared commitments promptly rather than forcing a transfer from nonexistent income.
A stable system values predictability over perfect monthly proportionality. Fairness can be reconciled over a quarter or year.

Set a maximum amount retained in the smoothing account and a rule for surplus above it. Otherwise variable income can accumulate without advancing shared goals or personal autonomy. For business owners, distinguish cash in the business from distributable household income; inventory, payroll and tax money are not available merely because the account balance is high. Share enough records to support the chosen owner draw, and obtain professional advice when entity rules or taxes make the calculation complex.

sections.heading: Separate Shared Goals From Individual Debt
paragraphs: List each debt with legal borrower, balance, rate, minimum, collateral and household consequence. Marriage or partnership does not automatically make every debt jointly contractual, though state law may create obligations. A shared spreadsheet should not mislabel liability. Obtain local advice for community-property, co-signed and jointly titled debts.

Decide whether pre-relationship debt is paid individually, supported indirectly through a lower shared contribution, or attacked as a household goal. Consider interest cost, effect on shared borrowing, moral commitments and each partner’s savings capacity. Whatever the choice, name it. Resentment grows when one person believes they are funding a shared future while the other believes a private debt is receiving household subsidy.

For new borrowing, require disclosure and an approval threshold before shared life is affected. Joint applicants can each be liable for the account. The CFPB explains that liability can differ between joint holders, co-signers and authorized users, and some responsibilities depend on state law.

Preserve minimum payments and starter reserves, then choose extra-payment priorities. The highest-rate approach can reduce cost; another sequence may improve cash flow or motivation. Do not use a debt method to punish the partner who earns less.
Track progress and release the old payment to a named goal when a balance closes.

Do not compare only balances. A low-rate student loan with protections may deserve a different priority from expensive revolving debt; a co-signed loan can create direct household exposure even when someone else receives the asset. Check credit reports so both partners understand accounts affecting shared borrowing. If one partner contributes extra to the other’s debt, specify whether that changes future shared contributions or ownership. In most households it should not create an informal claim that can be invoked later without prior agreement.

sections.heading: Price Housing to the Lower-Stress Standard
paragraphs: Housing often breaks an otherwise fair formula because the higher earner can afford a standard the lower earner cannot. Set a mutually affordable baseline based on contributions that leave both partners viable. If one person wants an upgrade, decide whether that partner funds the incremental rent, payment or maintenance without gaining unilateral control.

For renters, identify names on the lease, deposit ownership, utility responsibility and move-out consequences. For buyers, separate bill sharing from title and equity. Paying half the mortgage does not automatically create half ownership; contributing less does not necessarily mean no equitable claim under applicable law. Use a written co-ownership or cohabitation agreement reviewed locally before purchase.

Allocate repairs, furnishings and improvements explicitly. A couch is consumed differently from a roof replacement or principal payment. Record large transfers and purpose. Do not rely on a payment-app memo to resolve ownership years later.

Stress-test job loss and separation. Can either person carry the home temporarily? What notice, sale, refinance or buyout process applies? Who receives the deposit? An exit rule is not pessimism; it prevents housing security from becoming leverage.
Revisit after refinance, marriage, renovation or a major income shift. Housing is both shelter and a legal asset arrangement.

Calculate the standard using full housing cost: rent or debt service, taxes, insurance, association charges, utilities, parking, commuting and maintenance. A nominally proportional mortgage can still exhaust the lower earner when the location raises transport or childcare. If a room is reserved for one partner’s work, child or family, discuss the mixed benefit without turning square footage into hostile accounting. The agreement needs enough precision for major asymmetry, not a market rent assigned to every closet.

sections.heading: Coordinate Taxes, Benefits and Insurance Without Guessing
paragraphs: Married couples should compare filing choices using complete facts and current law. A joint return can create joint and individual responsibility for tax, interest and penalties. The [[S4|IRS explains]] that married filing separately changes liability and can change deductions and credits. Unmarried partners generally file under their own eligible statuses; household support and dependant rules require accurate application, not private allocation.

Decide how refunds or balances due are allocated before filing. A refund can reflect withholding, credits and liability from both partners; splitting it fifty-fifty may not reflect contributions or agreed household policy. Use a preparer or software capable of showing the components and preserve both partners’ review rights.

Compare employer health plans, retirement matches, dependent-care benefits and disability coverage as a household package. A plan with the lowest employee premium may have higher family out-of-pocket exposure. If one partner’s payroll carries family benefits, decide whether the premium is shared before calculating income contributions.

Review life insurance and beneficiaries when one partner depends on the other’s income or care. Unpaid household labor can create a replacement need even without salary. Confirm ownership and beneficiary forms separately from a will.
Tax and benefit optimization should not eliminate transparency. Both partners need records and enough understanding to act if the usual manager is unavailable.

Keep individual access to returns, benefit elections and policy documents. Each spouse signing a joint return should understand the reported income, deductions, credits, payments and refund destination. For employer enrollment, compare the next-best alternative rather than assuming one partner’s plan is free because the premium is payroll-deducted. Track open-enrollment and qualifying-event deadlines on a shared calendar. If one partner provides unpaid care, model the cost of replacing that care when evaluating life and disability protection.

sections.heading: Reconcile Monthly and Rewrite After Life Changes
paragraphs: The final photograph shows a couple holding cash and a receipt because a fair system needs a visible close. Hold a short monthly meeting with statements open. Compare planned shared costs, actual spending, transfers, upcoming irregular bills and progress toward goals. Reimburse documented exceptions and investigate recurring differences instead of arguing from memory.

Use a fixed agenda and stop time: facts, exceptions, next month, decisions and owners. Do not turn the meeting into a review of every personal purchase. Personal allowances remain personal. Shared overspending is a system issue; identify price changes, underestimated use or an unapproved commitment.

Create automatic recalculation triggers: income changes beyond a chosen band, parental leave, unemployment, disability, new child, elder care, move, marriage, separation or a major debt. Temporary changes need a start date, review date and end condition. Write whether extra support is a gift, shared obligation or repayable advance.

Maintain a one-page agreement: income definition, shared categories, split, account structure, labor allocation, personal allowances, goal transfers, approval threshold and review date. This is a household operating document, not necessarily a legal contract. Use counsel when ownership or legal rights require one.

The best split is not the one with the prettiest ratio. It is the one that funds shared life, preserves both partners’ resilience, recognizes labor, assigns legal responsibility accurately and can change without coercion.

End each meeting with a written decision log: issue, amount, owner, deadline and review trigger. Confirm transfers and reimbursements after execution. Quarterly, compare each partner’s remaining personal margin, reserve progress and unpaid labor—not just whether bills cleared. If one person repeatedly uses personal credit for shared expenses, the system is underfunded even when reimbursement eventually occurs. A fair plan should reduce emergency lending between partners and make support explicit before it becomes a grievance.

Audit the system annually from both perspectives. Calculate total shared cash contributed, personal margin retained, reserve and goal progress, debt change, major labor responsibilities and periods of income support. Numbers cannot measure every benefit, but they can reveal a pattern in which one partner always absorbs inflation, emergencies or career sacrifice. Ask each person privately what feels unfair, then compare answers without demanding immediate agreement. Preserve the parts that worked and rewrite the rule causing repeated exceptions. If the household is preparing for marriage, property purchase, parenthood or one partner leaving paid work, complete the review before the transition because bargaining power and legal exposure may change afterward. Keep a transition reserve in the name and account structure the partners intentionally select; do not assume shared savings will be accessible for every exit or emergency. Confirm who can stop automatic payments, change utilities, obtain tax records and communicate with a landlord or lender. A tested transition plan makes the everyday contribution system more trustworthy because neither partner must remain solely to preserve access to money, records or essential housing. Review that access together and in writing before every major shared commitment.

summary: Equal dollars are not automatically equal burden. Compare income capacity, essential obligations, employment risk and unpaid household work before adopting a split. Start with complete facts before debating percentages or defending a preferred rule. Keep the discussion voluntary and pause when facts need independent verification.

Classify expenses as shared, individual or negotiated before assigning percentages. Include irregular annual costs and require agreement before large or recurring commitments. Classify support obligations and blended-family costs explicitly instead of assigning them by default. A written unresolved category is safer than a silent assumption.

Define income consistently. Use dependable take-home capacity and decide symmetrically how retirement contributions, benefits, bonuses, business income and taxes are treated. Account for shared benefits already deducted from one partner’s paycheck. Review the income definition after benefits or payroll deductions change.

Calculate proportional shares from the defined income base, then test what each partner retains after shared costs and required individual obligations. Stress-test the ratio under an expensive month and a temporary income interruption. Round transfers consistently and document how the bills-account buffer is funded.

Adjust the baseline only for named facts such as unavoidable health costs, support duties, household location or a lifestyle upgrade requested by one partner. Agree which information is shared while preserving privacy for ordinary personal transactions. Shared visibility should never become surveillance of personal spending.

Keep contribution percentage separate from decision power. A higher cash contribution does not purchase greater control over shared choices. Include schedule control, on-call availability and rest when reviewing household labor. Outsourcing household work can protect time, careers and the relationship.

Preserve personal cash, individual access and independent credit identity where appropriate. Watch for financial control rather than treating coercion as a budget disagreement. Use institution-provided access and keep account ownership documents with emergency records. Account title and access rights matter during incapacity, death and separation.

Inventory childcare, cooking, cleaning, scheduling and caregiving. Decide whether to rebalance work, outsource it, reduce costs or adjust cash contributions. Keep business operating and tax cash separate from distributable household income. True up variable income on a predictable schedule using money already received.

Choose joint, separate or hybrid accounts based on function, legal ownership, access, records and autonomy—not as a test of loyalty. Specify whether extra debt help changes future contributions; never invent ownership afterward. Check legal liability before calling any debt shared or separate.

For variable income, fund recurring bills from a conservative base and reconcile above-base receipts after they arrive instead of creating monthly whiplash. Include transport, childcare, utilities and maintenance in the housing affordability standard. Complete ownership agreements before purchase rather than after a dispute.

List debts by legal borrower and household consequence. Decide explicitly whether pre-relationship obligations remain personal or become a shared payoff goal. Both partners should review tax returns, benefit elections and insurance documentation. Calendar enrollment and filing deadlines before choices become irreversible.

Set housing at a mutually sustainable standard. Separate monthly bill contributions from title, equity and legal ownership, especially for unmarried buyers. Use a decision log and verify every transfer after the meeting. Annual review should examine personal margin and labor as well as cleared bills.

Coordinate tax filing, benefits, insurance premiums and beneficiaries using current rules. Private spreadsheets do not override creditor, property or tax law. A higher earner can contribute more cash without receiving more authority. Support should be explicit before either partner relies on it.

Hold a short monthly reconciliation using statements and receipts. Review shared spending without policing purchases made from agreed personal allowances. A lower earner can contribute less cash without becoming financially dependent or uninformed. Equal decision power belongs in the agreement, not merely in conversation.

Write triggers for recalculation after income, leave, disability, caregiving, housing, marriage or separation changes. Recalculate after material changes, not as punishment for small monthly variation. Temporary changes need a review date and a clear end condition.

Maintain a one-page operating agreement covering income definition, categories, split, accounts, labor, allowances, approval limits and review date. Use qualified local advice whenever title, liability or marital law affects the arrangement. Keep evidence of large transfers, reimbursements and agreed exceptions.

The best system funds shared life while preserving both partners’ resilience, voice and accurate understanding of ownership and liability. The system succeeds when support is predictable, autonomy survives and neither partner carries hidden risk. No formula should require either partner to accept coercion or financial insecurity.

faq.question: Is a fifty-fifty split always unfair?
faq.answer: No. It can work when capacity, obligations and preferences align. The problem is treating it as automatically fair without testing burden.

faq.question: How do we calculate a proportional split?
faq.answer: Divide each partner’s consistently defined income by combined income, apply those shares to agreed shared costs and then test remaining capacity.

faq.question: Should unpaid housework reduce someone’s cash contribution?
faq.answer: It can, but the couple may instead rebalance tasks, outsource work or reduce spending. Use a task inventory rather than a vague assumption.

faq.question: Do joint accounts mean every dollar is legally half owned?
faq.answer: Not necessarily for every purpose. Account documents, state law, marital status and transaction facts matter. Obtain local advice for consequential ownership questions.

faq.question: How should bonuses be split?
faq.answer: Write a windfall sequence before payment arrives, including taxes, reserves, goals and personal allocation. Do not budget an uncertain bonus in advance.

faq.question: Should one partner help pay the other’s old debt?
faq.answer: That is a household choice. Compare cost, shared borrowing effects and each partner’s goals, then document whether support changes the bill split.

faq.question: How often should the formula change?
faq.answer: Review at least annually and after material income, family, health, caregiving or housing changes. Avoid recalculating for every small pay variation.

glossary.definition: Household contribution method tied to defined financial ability rather than equal dollars alone.
Cost both partners have explicitly agreed serves the household.
Agreed money each partner can use without transaction-level approval.
Holding variable receipts so recurring spending can use a stable base.
Account legally owned by more than one person under its documents and applicable law.
Person permitted to transact on an account without necessarily sharing the primary holder’s liability.
Planning, monitoring and coordination work required to keep household tasks operating.
Periodic reconciliation between planned contributions and actual eligible amounts.
Rule allowing an obligation to be collected from either responsible party under applicable law.
Agreement addressing financial or property arrangements between unmarried partners, subject to local law.
